Safety behaviors in aligned models are concentrated in a small subset of neurons, making alignment brittle and vulnerable to neuron-level attacks.
SafeNeuron significantly improves robustness against neuron pruning attacks and reduces the risk of open-source models being repurposed as red-team generators.
SafeNeuron preserves general model capabilities (e.g., on ARC, GSM8K, TruthfulQA) without introducing over-refusal.
Layer-wise and cross-task analysis reveals that safety behaviors are governed by stable and shared internal representations, including a core set of neurons active across diverse harmful tasks.
Iterative application of SafeNeuron progressively redistributes safety behaviors, constructing redundant safety pathways.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) and multimodal LLMs are typically safety-aligned before release to prevent harmful content generation. However, recent studies show that safety behaviors are concentrated in a small subset of parameters, making alignment brittle and easily bypassed through neuron-level attacks. Moreover, most existing alignment methods operate at the behavioral level, offering limited control over the model's internal safety mechanisms. In this work, we propose SafeNeuron, a neuron-level safety alignment framework that improves robustness by redistributing safety representations across the network. SafeNeuron first identifies safety-related neurons, then freezes these neurons during preference optimization to prevent reliance on sparse safety pathways and force the model to construct redundant safety representations. Extensive experiments across models and modalities demonstrate that SafeNeuron significantly improves robustness against neuron pruning attacks, reduces the risk of open-source models being repurposed as red-team generators, and preserves general capabilities. Furthermore, our layer-wise analysis reveals that safety behaviors are governed by stable and shared internal representations. Overall, SafeNeuron provides an interpretable and robust perspective for model alignment.

papers.title: Why Safeguarded Ships Run Aground? Aligned Large Language Models' Safety Mechanisms Tend to Be Anchored in The Template Region
papers.research_question: Why are aligned large language models vulnerable to jailbreak attacks? The paper hypothesizes that their safety mechanisms are overly reliant on the template region (Template-Anchored Safety Alignment).
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies Template-Anchored Safety Alignment (TASA) as a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, where safety mechanisms overly rely on the template region, and shows that detaching safety mechanisms from this region can mitigate jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: Template-anchored safety alignment is a widespread vulnerability in aligned LLMs, and future safety alignment techniques should reduce reliance on the template region to improve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Attention shifts from the instruction region to the template region when processing harmful inputs.
The template region has a causal effect on safety decisions, as shown by activation patching.
Intervening in the template region (TEMP PATCH) can jailbreak models with high success rates.
Jailbreak attacks suppress harmfulness features in the template region.
Harmfulness probes from the template region can be transferred to response generation to detect harmful content.
papers.limitation:
The analysis may not generalize to all safety-aligned LLMs, as some may have mitigated TASA through training data or feature suppression.
The proposed detachment method does not eliminate the learned safety shortcuts and is only a proof-of-concept.
future_direction: Develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.
Integrate adversarial defense patterns during training.
Proactively suppress shortcut-prone features during alignment.
papers.abstract: The safety alignment of large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable, as their initial behavior can be easily jailbroken by even relatively simple attacks. Since infilling a fixed template between the input instruction and initial model output is a common practice for existing LLMs, we hypothesize that this template is a key factor behind their vulnerabilities: LLMs' safety-related decision-making overly relies on the aggregated information from the template region, which largely influences these models' safety behavior. We refer to this issue as template-anchored safety alignment. In this paper, we conduct extensive experiments and verify that template-anchored safety alignment is widespread across various aligned LLMs. Our mechanistic analyses demonstrate how it leads to models' susceptibility when encountering inference-time jailbreak attacks. Furthermore, we show that detaching safety mechanisms from the template region is promising in mitigating vulnerabilities to jailbreak attacks. We encourage future research to develop more robust safety alignment techniques that reduce reliance on the template region.

papers.title: From Narrow Unlearning to Emergent Misalignment: Causes, Consequences, and Containment in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we steer the model away from refusal on a specific RAI concept using machine unlearning without causing emergent misalignment across other concepts? If emergent misalignment occurs, can we contain it? Can EMA be predicted by investigating the concept entanglements at representation level?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that narrow refusal unlearning can induce emergent misalignment (EMA) across unrelated responsible AI concepts, and proposes an augmented unlearning method that can partially restore alignment while maintaining low refusal rates on the target concept. It also shows that representation-level concept entanglement correlates with EMA.
papers.conclusion: This work extends the study of emergent misalignment (EMA) by investigating machine unlearning as an alternative baseline for steering aligned models on targeted domains. While narrow refusal unlearning can substantially reduce refusals on the intervened concept, it is also prone to EMA. Augmenting refusal unlearning with cross-entropy loss on retain sets can largely restore alignment across impacted domains, and representation-level analysis reveals a correlation between concept overlap and EMA.
papers.key_findings:
Narrow refusal unlearning effectively reduces refusals on a target concept but can cause emergent misalignment (reduced refusals) in other unrelated concepts.
The safety concept intervention has a larger EMA impact (causing lower refusal scores across more domains) compared to cybersecurity.
Augmenting refusal unlearning with cross-entropy loss on retain sets from affected domains can largely restore alignment in those domains, though not always fully.
Concept entanglement at the representation level (using concept vectors) shows that concepts with higher similarity in early layers are more susceptible to EMA after intervention.
The phenomenon of EMA is consistent across two model families (Mistral and Qwen).
papers.limitation:
Experiments were limited to two concepts (Cybersecurity and Safety) and two instruction-tuned aligned models (Qwen-7B-2.5 and Mistral-7B) due to computational resources.
A simplistic training-free approach (concept vectors) was used to investigate concept entanglement; more sophisticated training-based techniques (e.g., Sparse Autoencoders) could provide deeper insight.
Evaluation covers seven RAI concepts but a deeper analysis of the model's internal dynamics (e.g., model diffing) to assess cross-concept generalization effects is deferred to future work.
future_direction: Evaluating refusal unlearning on larger-scale models.
Using more sophisticated training-based techniques (e.g., Sparse Autoencoders) to analyze RAI concept entanglements.
Analyzing internal dynamics (e.g., model diffing) to assess cross-concept generalization effects.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that fine-tuning on insecure code data can trigger an emergent misalignment (EMA) phenomenon, where models generate malicious responses even to prompts unrelated to the original insecure code-writing task. Such cross-domain generalization of harmful behavior underscores the need for a deeper understanding of the algorithms, tasks, and datasets that induce emergent misalignment. In this work, we extend this study by demonstrating that emergent misalignment can also arise from narrow refusal unlearning in specific domains. We perform refusal unlearning on Cybersecurity and Safety concept, and evaluate EMA by monitoring refusal scores across seven responsible AI (RAI) domains, Cybersecurity, Safety, Toxicity, Bias, Sensitive Content, Medical/Legal, and Privacy. Our work shows that narrow domain unlearning can yield compliance responses for the targeted concept, however, it may also propagate EMA to unrelated domains. Among the two intervened concepts, Cybersecurity and Safety, we find that the safety concept can have larger EMA impact, i.e, causing lower refusal scores, across other unrelated domains such as bias. We observe this effect consistently across two model families, Mistral-7b-0.3v, and Qwen-7b-2.5. Further, we show that refusal unlearning augmented with cross-entropy loss function on a small set of retain data from the affected domains can largely, if not fully, restore alignment across the impacted domains while having lower refusal rate on the concept we perform unlearning on. To investigate the underlying causes of EMA, we analyze concept entanglements at the representation level via concept vectors. Our analysis reveals that concepts with higher representation similarity in earlier layers are more susceptible to EMA after intervention when the refusal stream is altered through targeted refusal unlearning.

papers.title: Navigating the OverKill in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What factors contribute to overkill (excessive refusal to answer benign queries) in large language models, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Self-Contrastive Decoding (Self-CD), a training-free and model-agnostic method that reduces overkill in LLMs by mitigating shortcuts in attention to harmful words, achieving lower refusal rates without compromising safety.
papers.conclusion: The paper defines overkill in LLMs and proposes Self-CD, a simple and effective method that significantly reduces refusal rates without training, addressing shortcuts in model attention.
papers.key_findings:
Models exhibit shortcuts, leading to over-attention to harmful words like 'kill', regardless of query semantics.
Safety-emphasized system prompts exacerbate overkill by increasing reliance on shortcuts.
Self-CD reduces refusal rates by an average of 20% across models while maintaining safety.
Overkill is widespread across various models, independent of size or architecture.
Models have a superficial understanding of user queries, relying on word-level cues rather than full semantics.
papers.limitation: Incomplete availability of training data for large models limits further research.
future_direction: Analyze biases or toxicity in human feedback datasets.
Investigate shortcuts or misgeneralizations in reward models.
papers.abstract: Large language models are meticulously aligned to be both helpful and harmless. However, recent research points to a potential overkill which means models may refuse to answer benign queries. In this paper, we investigate the factors for overkill by exploring how models handle and determine the safety of queries. Our findings reveal the presence of shortcuts within models, leading to an over-attention of harmful words like 'kill' and prompts emphasizing safety will exacerbate overkill. Based on these insights, we introduce Self-Contrastive Decoding (Self-CD), a training-free and model-agnostic strategy, to alleviate this phenomenon. We first extract such over-attention by amplifying the difference in the model's output distributions when responding to system prompts that either include or omit an emphasis on safety. Then we determine the final next-token predictions by downplaying the over-attention from the model via contrastive decoding. Empirical results indicate that our method has achieved an average reduction of the refusal rate by 20\% while having almost no impact on safety.

papers.title: Improving LLM Safety Alignment with Dual-Objective Optimization
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) in safety alignment, and how can they be addressed with a dual-objective optimization approach?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces DOOR, a dual-objective optimization method that combines robust refusal training and targeted unlearning to improve LLM safety alignment against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: DOOR and W-DOOR improve LLM safety alignment by combining refusal training and unlearning, achieving better robustness against jailbreaks while maintaining utility.
papers.key_findings:
DOOR addresses limitations of DPO by providing a constant learning rate for safe responses, improving refusal learning.
W-DOOR with token-level weighting further enhances robustness by emphasizing critical refusal tokens.
The methods significantly reduce attack success rates across prefilling, suffix, and multi-turn jailbreak attacks.
Robustness is correlated with token distribution shifts in the training process and internal representations.
The approach maintains general model utility while improving safety, as shown on benchmarks like HellaSwag.
papers.limitation:
Token-level weighting parameters could be better optimized and stabilized.
Current data augmentation techniques may lead to overrefusal from falsely learned transitions.
future_direction: Optimizing token-level weighting parameters and stabilizing reward designs.
Developing advanced data augmentation techniques to reduce overrefusal.
Investigating robustness of DOOR and W-DOOR to other jailbreak attack types.
papers.abstract: Existing training-time safety alignment techniques for large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Direct preference optimization (DPO), a widely deployed alignment method, exhibits limitations in both experimental and theoretical contexts as its loss function proves suboptimal for refusal learning. Through gradient-based analysis, we identify these shortcomings and propose an improved safety alignment that disentangles DPO objectives into two components: (1) robust refusal training, which encourages refusal even when partial unsafe generations are produced, and (2) targeted unlearning of harmful knowledge. This approach significantly increases LLM robustness against a wide range of jailbreak attacks, including prefilling, suffix, and multi-turn attacks across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios. Furthermore, we introduce a method to emphasize critical refusal tokens by incorporating a reward-based token-level weighting mechanism for refusal learning, which further improves the robustness against adversarial exploits. Our research also suggests that robustness to jailbreak attacks is correlated with token distribution shifts in the training process and internal representations of refusal and harmful tokens, offering valuable directions for future research in LLM safety alignment. The code is available at https://github.com/wicai24/DOOR-Alignment

papers.title: Safety Layers in Aligned Large Language Models: The Key to LLM Security
papers.research_question: What is the internal mechanism (safety layers) that enables aligned LLMs to recognize malicious queries, and how can we fine-tune these models without degrading their security?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies safety layers in aligned LLMs that are crucial for security and proposes SPPFT, a fine-tuning method that freezes these layers to preserve security while maintaining performance.
papers.conclusion: Safety layers are the key to LLM security, and freezing them during fine-tuning via SPPFT effectively prevents security degradation while preserving performance.
papers.key_findings:
Aligned LLMs contain a small set of contiguous middle layers, called safety layers, that are crucial for distinguishing malicious from normal queries.
Safety layers emerge as a result of security alignment; pre-trained LLMs do not exhibit such layers.
Scaling the parameters of safety layers amplifies or diminishes the model's security, as measured by over-rejection.
The proposed SPPFT method, which freezes safety layers during fine-tuning, significantly preserves security while maintaining performance and reducing computational cost.
Freezing layers other than the safety layers does not effectively protect security, confirming the specificity of safety layers.
papers.abstract: Aligned LLMs are secure, capable of recognizing and refusing to answer malicious questions. However, the role of internal parameters in maintaining such security is not well understood yet, further these models can be vulnerable to security degradation when subjected to fine-tuning attacks. To address these challenges, our work uncovers the mechanism behind security in aligned LLMs at the parameter level, identifying a small set of contiguous layers in the middle of the model that are crucial for distinguishing malicious queries from normal ones, referred to as ``safety layers". We first confirm the existence of these safety layers by analyzing variations in input vectors within the model's internal layers. Additionally, we leverage the over-rejection phenomenon and parameters scaling analysis to precisely locate the safety layers. Building on these findings, we propose a novel fine-tuning approach, Safely Partial-Parameter Fine-Tuning (SPPFT), that fixes the gradient of the safety layers during fine-tuning to address the security degradation. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly preserve LLM security while maintaining performance and reducing computational resources compared to full fine-tuning.

papers.title: CLUE: Conflict-guided Localization for LLM Unlearning Framework
papers.research_question: How can we improve LLM unlearning by precisely localizing neurons responsible for forgetting and retaining, using circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CLUE, a framework that uses circuit discovery and CNF satisfiability to localize forget, retain, and conflict neurons for targeted unlearning, improving forget efficacy and retain utility.
papers.conclusion: CLUE offers more precise neuron localization and significantly outperforms existing methods in both forget efficacy and retain utility.
papers.key_findings:
CLUE outperforms existing localization methods in forget efficacy and retain utility with fewer modified parameters.
It successfully identifies forget, retain, and conflict neurons through CNF satisfiability of circuits.
The proportion of forget neurons increases and conflict neurons decreases after unlearning, indicating effective decoupling.
Circuit sparsity and faithfulness are correlated with unlearning efficacy.
CLUE provides more comprehensive interpretability by revealing neuron categories and their distributions.
papers.limitation:
The circuit is static and cannot dynamically reflect changes in key neurons during the fine-tuning process.
For multiple retain sets, the fine-tuning stage cannot provide targeted solutions for every possible conflict combination.
future_direction: Exploring the dynamics of circuits during parameter fine-tuning.
Developing editing methods other than fine-tuning for multiple retain sets.
papers.abstract: The LLM unlearning aims to eliminate the influence of undesirable data without affecting causally unrelated information. This process typically involves using a forget set to remove target information, alongside a retain set to maintain non-target capabilities. While recent localization-based methods demonstrate promise in identifying important neurons to be unlearned, they fail to disentangle neurons responsible for forgetting undesirable knowledge or retaining essential skills, often treating them as a single entangled group. As a result, these methods apply uniform interventions, risking catastrophic over-forgetting or incomplete erasure of the target knowledge. To address this, we turn to circuit discovery, a mechanistic interpretability technique, and propose the Conflict-guided Localization for LLM Unlearning framEwork (CLUE). This framework identifies the forget and retain circuit composed of important neurons, and then the circuits are transformed into conjunctive normal forms (CNF). The assignment of each neuron in the CNF satisfiability solution reveals whether it should be forgotten or retained. We then provide targeted fine-tuning strategies for different categories of neurons. Extensive experiments demonstrate that, compared to existing localization methods, CLUE achieves superior forget efficacy and retain utility through precise neural localization.

papers.title: Latent Adversarial Training Improves the Representation of Refusal
papers.research_question: How does Latent Adversarial Training (LAT) affect the underlying representation of refusal behavior in language models compared to supervised safety fine-tuning (SSFT) and embedding space adversarial training (AT)?
papers.core_contribution: LAT reorganizes refusal behavior in the latent space, concentrating it in the first two SVD components, which leads to more effective and transferable refusal vectors for ablation attacks but also increases vulnerability to self-generated vectors.
papers.conclusion: LAT significantly alters the encoding of refusal behavior in the latent space, creating a more concentrated representation that is effective for cross-model attacks but vulnerable to self-attacks, highlighting both strengths and vulnerabilities for improving model safety.
papers.key_findings:
LAT concentrates refusal representation in the first two SVD components, explaining approximately 75% of activation differences variance.
LAT models show lower resistance to self-generated refusal ablation attacks compared to SSFT and AT.
LAT refusal vectors are more effective and transferable across different model variants.
LAT does not substantially redistribute refusal representation across network layers; layer 14 remains most effective for ablation.
LAT's training perturbations enable a more comprehensive representation of refusal behavior, but make models more vulnerable to self-attacks.
papers.limitation:
Uncertainty about the exact semantic meaning of the identified directions in the latent space.
Experiments conducted exclusively on Llama-2-7B-chat, limiting generalizability to other architectures or scales.
Focus on a specific ablation technique without comprehensive evaluation of other adversarial attacks or activation steering methods.
Limited to harmful and harmless examples from the AdvBench and Alpaca datasets.
future_direction: Focus on maintaining LAT's robust representations while addressing its susceptibility to ablation attacks.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that language models' refusal behavior is primarily encoded in a single direction in their latent space, making it vulnerable to targeted attacks. Although Latent Adversarial Training (LAT) attempts to improve robustness by introducing noise during training, a key question remains: How does this noise-based training affect the underlying representation of refusal behavior? Understanding this encoding is crucial for evaluating LAT's effectiveness and limitations, just as the discovery of linear refusal directions revealed vulnerabilities in traditional supervised safety fine-tuning (SSFT). Through the analysis of Llama 2 7B, we examine how LAT reorganizes the refusal behavior in the model's latent space compared to SSFT and embedding space adversarial training (AT). By computing activation differences between harmful and harmless instruction pairs and applying Singular Value Decomposition (SVD), we find that LAT significantly alters the refusal representation, concentrating it in the first two SVD components which explain approximately 75 percent of the activation differences variance - significantly higher than in reference models. This concentrated representation leads to more effective and transferable refusal vectors for ablation attacks: LAT models show improved robustness when attacked with vectors from reference models but become more vulnerable to self-generated vectors compared to SSFT and AT. Our findings suggest that LAT's training perturbations enable a more comprehensive representation of refusal behavior, highlighting both its potential strengths and vulnerabilities for improving model safety.

papers.title: Circuit-Aware Reward Training: A Mechanistic Framework for Longtail Robustness in RLHF
papers.research_question: What is the role of neural circuit specialization in reward models for longtail robustness, and how can it be leveraged to prevent reward hacking?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a mechanistic interpretability framework to identify and mitigate longtail vulnerabilities in reward models through circuit-aware training.
papers.conclusion: Reward hacking is a mechanistic failure due to longtail circuit specialization, and CART connects mechanistic interpretability with practical alignment to improve robustness.
papers.key_findings:
Reward models develop specialized neural circuits for processing rare preference scenarios.
Longtail generalization error is bounded by the number of specialized circuits and their divergence from common circuits.
Vulnerable circuits can be identified through activation patterns, coherence analysis, and causal validation.
Circuit-Aware Reward Training (CART) uses targeted interventions like data augmentation and regularization to improve robustness.
CART provides a principled framework for connecting circuit specialization to reward model failures.
papers.limitation:
Mechanistic interpretability methods are computationally intensive, raising scalability concerns.
Circuits may not always exhibit clean specialization, as networks often have overlapping or dynamic structures.
Evaluating robustness on longtail scenarios is difficult, requiring new benchmarks and protocols.
Extension to other modalities such as vision, robotics, or multimodal alignment remains an open question.
future_direction: Extending the framework to other modalities like vision and robotics.
Developing new benchmarks and protocols for evaluating longtail robustness.
papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) reward models exhibit systematic failures on longtail distributions, leading to reward hacking and misalignment. We propose a mechanistic interpretability framework that identifies specialized neural circuits responsible for rare-event processing in reward models. Drawing from recent advances showing distributed specialization for rare tokens in language models\citep{liu2025no, liu2025emergent}, we hypothesize that reward models also develop functionally distinct circuits for longtail scenarios. Our theoretical framework establishes formal connections between circuit specialization, reward generalization bounds, and longtail performance. We introduce \textbf{Circuit-Aware Reward Training (CART)}, which uses circuit analysis to guide data augmentation, regularization, and ensemble strategies. This approach provides both theoretical insights into reward model failures and practical interventions for improving longtail robustness.

papers.title: Locking Down the Finetuned LLMs Safety
papers.research_question: How can we locate safety-relevant attention heads in a large scale of fine-tuned models and effectively obtain the safety vector for fine-tuned LLMs without negative transfer to other general tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SafetyLock, a method to maintain safety in fine-tuned LLMs by extracting safety directions (Meta-SafetyLock) from the base model and applying them to fine-tuned models via activation intervention.
papers.conclusion: SafetyLock is an efficient method for maintaining the safety of fine-tuned LLMs, offering a scalable and effective approach to aligning models with ethical constraints while preserving utility.
papers.key_findings:
SafetyLock reduces the harmful instruction response rate from 60% to below 1% in toxic fine-tuned models.
SafetyLock can be applied in under 0.01 seconds without additional computational cost.
The safety-related activation patterns are largely preserved during fine-tuning, enabling transferable safety interventions.
SafetyLock maintains model performance on general tasks while significantly improving safety.
The method demonstrates robust defense against both fine-tuning vulnerabilities and prompt-based attacks.
future_direction: Explore SafetyLock's applicability to other model architectures.
Investigate its potential in multi-modal settings.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on additional datasets is often necessary to optimize them for specific downstream tasks. However, existing safety alignment measures, which restrict harmful behavior during inference, are insufficient to mitigate safety risks during fine-tuning. Alarmingly, fine-tuning with just 10 toxic sentences can make models comply with harmful instructions. We introduce SafetyLock, a novel alignment intervention method that maintains robust safety post-fine-tuning through efficient and transferable mechanisms. SafetyLock leverages our discovery that fine-tuned models retain similar safety-related activation representations to their base models. This insight enables us to extract what we term the Meta-SafetyLock, a set of safety bias directions representing key activation patterns associated with safe responses in the original model. We can then apply these directions universally to fine-tuned models to enhance their safety. By searching for activation directions across multiple token dimensions, SafetyLock achieves enhanced robustness and transferability. SafetyLock re-aligns fine-tuned models in under 0.01 seconds without additional computational cost. Our experiments demonstrate that SafetyLock can reduce the harmful instruction response rate from 60% to below 1% in toxic fine-tuned models. It surpasses traditional methods in both performance and efficiency, offering a scalable, non-invasive solution for ensuring the safety of customized LLMs. Our analysis across various fine-tuning scenarios confirms SafetyLock's robustness, advocating its integration into safety protocols for aligned LLMs. The code is released at https://github.com/zhu-minjun/SafetyLock.

papers.title: RepIt: Steering Language Models with Concept-Specific Refusal Vectors
papers.research_question: How can we isolate concept-specific refusal representations in language model activations to enable targeted jailbreaks while preserving refusal on other harmful concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces REPIT, a framework to isolate concept-specific refusal representations in LM activations, enabling targeted jailbreaks that evade standard safety benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: The REPIT framework demonstrates precise concept disentanglement, exposing vulnerabilities in current safety evaluation practices and highlighting the need for more comprehensive, representation-aware assessments.
papers.key_findings:
REPIT can jailbreak target concepts (e.g., weapons of mass destruction) while preserving refusal on non-target harmful concepts, achieving high target attack success rates with minimal spillover.
The edit to the steering vector localizes to just 100-200 neurons, indicating a sparse, high-leverage mechanism.
REPIT is highly data-efficient, producing robust concept vectors from as few as 12 target examples.
Standard safety benchmarks fail to detect models with such targeted, concept-specific jailbreaks, revealing a critical evaluation blind spot.
Disentanglement reveals that target and non-target refusal representations are entangled, and the removed projection can itself induce jailbreaks.
papers.limitation: COSMIC only supports a binary harmful/harmless setup, requiring adaptation for the target/non-target/harmless formulation.
future_direction: Further research using SAE or circuit perspectives to understand the bidirectional effects and heavy-tail neuron phenomena.
Development of more comprehensive, representation-aware safety assessments.
papers.abstract: While activation steering in large language models (LLMs) is a growing area of research, methods can often incur broader effects than desired. This motivates isolation of purer concept vectors to enable targeted interventions and understand LLM behavior at a more granular level. We present RepIt, a simple and data-efficient framework for isolating concept-specific representations. Across five frontier LLMs, RepIt enables precise interventions: it selectively suppresses refusal on targeted concepts while preserving refusal elsewhere, producing models that answer WMD-related questions while still scoring as safe on standard benchmarks. We further show that the corrective signal localizes to just 100-200 neurons and that robust target representations can be extracted from as few as a dozen examples on a single A6000. This efficiency raises a dual concern: manipulations can be performed with modest compute and data to extend to underrepresented data-scarce topics while evading existing benchmarks. By disentangling refusal vectors with RepIt, this work demonstrates that targeted interventions can counteract overgeneralization, laying the foundation for more granular control of model behavior.

papers.title: Towards Understanding and Improving Refusal in Compressed Models via Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: How does the refusal mechanism change in compressed models, and why are quantized models safer than pruned ones? Additionally, how can we improve the safety of compressed models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that compressed models retain a single-direction refusal mechanism, but pruning alters this direction leading to safety loss, and introduces AIRD to improve safety of compressed models without performance degradation.
papers.conclusion: The refusal mechanism changes in pruned models, explaining safety loss, and AIRD can effectively improve safety without harming performance.
papers.key_findings:
The refusal mechanism is still mediated by a single direction in compressed models.
In pruned models, the source position of the refusal direction changes, while in quantized models it remains the same.
The change in refusal direction correlates with loss of safety in pruned models.
Quantized models are safer than pruned models because they retain the original refusal direction.
AIRD can improve safety of pruned models without significant performance loss.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not generalize to non-transformer architectures like Mixture of Experts, State Space Models, and RNNs.
AIRD reduces the compression rate by decreasing sparsity in one layer.
future_direction: Generalize findings to non-transformer architectures.
Optimize AIRD to mitigate compression rate reduction.
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of large language models has spurred significant interest in model compression as a means to enhance their accessibility and practicality. While extensive research has explored model compression through the lens of safety, findings suggest that safety-aligned models often lose elements of trustworthiness post-compression. Simultaneously, the field of mechanistic interpretability has gained traction, with notable discoveries, such as the identification of a single direction in the residual stream mediating refusal behaviors across diverse model architectures. In this work, we investigate the safety of compressed models by examining the mechanisms of refusal, adopting a novel interpretability-driven perspective to evaluate model safety. Furthermore, leveraging insights from our interpretability analysis, we propose a lightweight, computationally efficient method to enhance the safety of compressed models without compromising their performance or utility.

papers.title: Interpretability in the Wild: a Circuit for Indirect Object Identification in GPT-2 small
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 small perform the indirect object identification (IOI) task, and what internal circuit is responsible for this behavior?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies and validates a circuit of 26 attention heads in GPT-2 small that performs indirect object identification, using a combination of interpretability techniques and quantitative criteria for faithfulness, completeness, and minimality.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, providing a step towards scaling interpretability to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Discovered a circuit of 26 attention heads grouped into 7 classes (e.g., Name Mover Heads, S-Inhibition Heads) that implement the IOI task.
Identified redundant behavior such as Backup Name Mover Heads that activate when regular Name Mover Heads are ablated.
Found that Negative Name Mover Heads write in the opposite direction, potentially to hedge predictions.
Formulated and evaluated quantitative criteria (faithfulness, completeness, minimality) to validate circuit explanations.
The circuit shows significant but incomplete understanding, with gaps in completeness and minimality.
papers.limitation:
Not fully understanding some components, such as the attention patterns of S-Inhibition Heads and the role of MLPs and layer norms.
The circuit is not completely complete or minimal, as shown by quantitative criteria.
The analysis is limited to GPT-2 small, which is much smaller than state-of-the-art models.
future_direction: Scale the approach to larger models like GPT-2 medium.
Investigate the behavior of the circuit on adversarial examples.
Understand the compensation effect in Backup Name Mover Heads.
papers.abstract: Research in mechanistic interpretability seeks to explain behaviors of machine learning models in terms of their internal components. However, most previous work either focuses on simple behaviors in small models, or describes complicated behaviors in larger models with broad strokes. In this work, we bridge this gap by presenting an explanation for how GPT-2 small performs a natural language task called indirect object identification (IOI). Our explanation encompasses 26 attention heads grouped into 7 main classes, which we discovered using a combination of interpretability approaches relying on causal interventions. To our knowledge, this investigation is the largest end-to-end attempt at reverse-engineering a natural behavior "in the wild" in a language model. We evaluate the reliability of our explanation using three quantitative criteria--faithfulness, completeness and minimality. Though these criteria support our explanation, they also point to remaining gaps in our understanding. Our work provides evidence that a mechanistic understanding of large ML models is feasible, opening opportunities to scale our understanding to both larger models and more complex tasks.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Large Reasoning Models: A Survey of Training, Inference, and Failures
papers.research_question: What are the internal mechanisms that drive the reasoning behaviors and failures of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: This survey synthesizes recent research on the mechanistic understanding of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), organizing insights into training dynamics, reasoning mechanisms, and unintended behaviors to bridge the gap between performance and transparency.
papers.conclusion: The survey highlights the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework to advance the mechanistic understanding of LRMs.
papers.key_findings:
SFT expands exploratory paths while RL compresses them, leading to entropy reduction and performance gains.
RL training follows a two-stage process where basic skills are acquired first, followed by the emergence of reasoning abilities.
LRMs exhibit unique reasoning structures, including cyclical processes and topological properties, driven by key behavioral primitives.
Hallucinations in LRMs are influenced by RL, which reduces abstention and can increase incorrect answers.
Chain-of-thought reasoning in LRMs is often unfaithful, with a disconnect between internal states and verbalized traces.
papers.limitation:
The rapid development of LRM research means that new findings may not be captured in this survey.
The survey focuses primarily on language models, excluding multimodal capabilities.
The discussion is limited to traditional LLM architectures, excluding newer approaches like diffusion-based LLMs.
future_direction: Applied interpretability for training-time and inference-time improvements
Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: Re-Emergent Misalignment: How Narrow Fine-Tuning Erodes Safety Alignment in LLMs
papers.research_question: How does narrow fine-tuning (e.g., on insecure code) lead to broad misalignment in LLMs, and is this due to emergent misalignment or erosion of prior alignment?
papers.core_contribution: Narrow fine-tuning on insecure code erodes prior alignment by weakening shared internal safety mechanisms, rather than creating novel misaligned behaviors.
papers.conclusion: Misalignment from narrow fine-tuning is better understood as erosion of prior alignment, highlighting the fragility of alignment and the need for more robust fine-tuning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
The misaligned model assigns similar probabilities to harmful sequences as the base model, suggesting a reversion to pre-alignment behavior.
Loss and gradient signals for insecure code and educational insecure are opposing, indicating the model internalizes behavioral intent from prompt framing.
Activation projections show the misaligned model's representations drift from instruct-like to base-like patterns in deeper layers.
A shared latent direction in activation space links insecure code and toxic generations, explaining why narrow fine-tuning leads to broad misalignment.
Alignment erosion is a general effect, observed across multiple datasets, not specific to the insecure code domain.
papers.limitation: The observed opposing learning signals between datasets could be driven by structural differences, providing suggestive but not definitive causal evidence of alignment erosion.
future_direction: Develop alignment techniques that identify alignment-critical subspaces and measure representational drift.
Apply structural constraints to prevent erosion of safety-relevant mechanisms during continued training.
Build alignment frameworks that treat internal model structure as a first-class target of analysis and intervention.
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on code with security vulnerabilities can result in misaligned and unsafe behaviors across broad domains. These results prompted concerns about the emergence of harmful behaviors from narrow domain fine-tuning. In this paper, we contextualize these findings by analyzing how such narrow adaptation impacts the internal mechanisms and behavioral manifestations of LLMs. Through a series of experiments covering output probability distributions, loss and gradient vector geometry, layer-wise activation dynamics, and activation space dimensions, we find that behaviors attributed to "emergent misalignment" may be better interpreted as an erosion of prior alignment. We show that fine tuning on insecure code induces internal changes that oppose alignment. Further, we identify a shared latent dimension in the model's activation space that governs alignment behavior. We show that this space is activated by insecure code and by misaligned responses more generally, revealing how narrow fine-tuning can degrade general safety behavior by interfering with shared internal mechanisms. Our findings offer a mechanistic interpretation for previously observed misalignment phenomena, and highlights the fragility of alignment in LLMs. The results underscore the need for more robust fine-tuning strategies that preserve intended behavior across domains.

papers.title: ARREST: Adversarial Resilient Regulation Enhancing Safety and Truth in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do multi-head attention mechanisms and internal representations govern both safety and hallucination behaviors in LLMs? Can an external network correct representational misalignment without fine-tuning the model parameters?
papers.core_contribution: ARREST is a unified framework that addresses safety and hallucination in LLMs by correcting representational misalignment in internal activations using adversarial training, without fine-tuning the model parameters.
papers.conclusion: ARREST effectively tackles safety alignment and hallucination mitigation by focusing on representational misalignment, offering a lightweight intervention approach.
papers.key_findings:
ARREST improves factual accuracy across multiple datasets compared to base models and other baselines.
It reduces attack success rates for safety benchmarks and increases soft refusal rates.
ARREST generates context-aware soft refusals, unlike hard refusals from RLHF-aligned models.
It requires training only ~33M parameters instead of full fine-tuning.
PCA visualizations show that ARREST shifts internal representations towards aligned distributions.
papers.limitation:
ARREST relies on the quality and coverage of its adversarial training data.
It introduces dual-use risks as similar mechanisms could induce undesirable behaviors.
Interpretability concerns due to the added regulator.
future_direction: Investigate the extent to which soft refusals dominate model behavior.
Explore applicability to broader LLM alignment objectives.
papers.abstract: Human cognition, driven by complex neurochemical processes, oscillates between imagination and reality and learns to self-correct whenever such subtle drifts lead to hallucinations or unsafe associations. In recent years, LLMs have demonstrated remarkable performance in a wide range of tasks. However, they still lack human cognition to balance factuality and safety. Bearing the resemblance, we argue that both factual and safety failures in LLMs arise from a representational misalignment in their latent activation space, rather than addressing those as entirely separate alignment issues. We hypothesize that an external network, trained to understand the fluctuations, can selectively intervene in the model to regulate falsehood into truthfulness and unsafe output into safe output without fine-tuning the model parameters themselves. Reflecting the hypothesis, we propose ARREST (Adversarial Resilient Regulation Enhancing Safety and Truth), a unified framework that identifies and corrects drifted features, engaging both soft and hard refusals in addition to factual corrections. Our empirical results show that ARREST not only regulates misalignment but is also more versatile compared to the RLHF-aligned models in generating soft refusals due to adversarial training. We make our codebase available at https://github.com/sharanya-dasgupta001/ARREST.

papers.title: Head-Specific Intervention Can Induce Misaligned AI Coordination in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Can inference-time activation interventions at specific attention heads bypass safety alignments and steer LLMs towards harmful AI coordination?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Head-Specific Intervention (HSI), a method that uses attention-head-level probing and intervention to steer LLM behavior, showing it can effectively induce misaligned AI coordination and outperforms layer-wise interventions and fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: HSI is an effective method for steering LLM behavior, demonstrating that activations at specific attention heads encode fine-grained linearly separable behaviors and that current alignment techniques can be bypassed without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
HSI can bypass safety alignments and steer models towards harmful AI coordination.
HSI generalizes from binary choice to open-ended generation settings.
HSI is more effective than intervening on full layers or supervised fine-tuning.
Only a few example completions are needed to compute effective steering directions.
Applying interventions in the negative direction can prevent a common jailbreak attack.
papers.limitation:
If intervention directions vary significantly between examples, calculating the mean across positive and negative labels may produce a direction that is ineffective for steering the model.
Sweeping over all attention heads could become computationally expensive for larger models with more attention heads.
future_direction: Further optimization of the technique to identify patterns and relevant heads without sweeping over all model components.
Extend evaluation to a broader range of models with more substantial differences in pre-training data, fine-tuning procedures, and architectural design.
Investigate alignment patterns within model activations and reasons for opposing directions in outlier examples to refine intervention methods.
papers.abstract: Robust alignment guardrails for large language models (LLMs) are becoming increasingly important with their widespread application. In contrast to previous studies, we demonstrate that inference-time activation interventions can bypass safety alignments and effectively steer model generations towards harmful AI coordination. Our method applies fine-grained interventions at specific attention heads, which we identify by probing each head in a simple binary choice task. We then show that interventions on these heads generalise to the open-ended generation setting, effectively circumventing safety guardrails. We demonstrate that intervening on a few attention heads is more effective than intervening on full layers or supervised fine-tuning. We further show that only a few example completions are needed to compute effective steering directions, which is an advantage over classical fine-tuning. We also demonstrate that applying interventions in the negative direction can prevent a common jailbreak attack. Our results suggest that, at the attention head level, activations encode fine-grained linearly separable behaviours. Practically, the approach offers a straightforward methodology to steer large language model behaviour, which could be extended to diverse domains beyond safety, requiring fine-grained control over the model output. The code and datasets for this study can be found on https://github.com/PaulDrm/targeted_intervention.

papers.title: The Side Effects of Being Smart: Safety Risks in MLLMs' Multi-Image Reasoning
papers.research_question: Do improved capabilities in multi-image reasoning expand the attack surface and introduce new safety risks in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs)?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MIR-SafetyBench, the first benchmark for evaluating multi-image reasoning safety in MLLMs, and finds that models with stronger multi-image reasoning capabilities are often more vulnerable to safety attacks, with unsafe generations exhibiting lower attention entropy.
papers.conclusion: The paper introduces MIR-SafetyBench and demonstrates extensive safety risks in MLLMs during multi-image reasoning, highlighting the need for improved safety alignment in complex multimodal scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-image relational attacks succeed widely across 19 MLLMs, with the highest Attack Success Rate (ASR) reaching 87.63%.
Within a broad range of models, stronger multi-image reasoning capability correlates with higher ASR, indicating a capability-safety trade-off.
Many safe responses are superficial, arising from misunderstanding, generic refusals, or evasive answers rather than robust safety alignment.
In multi-image scenarios, unsafe generations exhibit lower attention entropy than safe ones on average, suggesting models may over-focus on task solving while neglecting safety constraints.
Multi-image relational prompts lead to significantly higher ASR compared to single-image prompts for the same harmful intent.
papers.limitation:
Benchmark coverage is not exhaustive and may inherit biases from source datasets and the automated pipeline.
Dependence on automatic components (e.g., DeepSeek-R1, FLUX.1-dev, HarmBench classifier) may introduce systematic noise.
Evaluation is limited to a fixed set of models under single-turn prompting, and attention-entropy analysis provides only correlational evidence.
The work is diagnostic rather than prescriptive, with no concrete mitigation mechanisms proposed.
future_direction: Extend MIR-SafetyBench to more realistic user interactions, additional modalities and relation types, and richer measurements of internal states and real-world safety impact.
Bridge the gap from characterization to practical mitigation with detection mechanisms, safety monitors, or training-time regularizers.
papers.abstract: As Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) acquire stronger reasoning capabilities to handle complex, multi-image instructions, this advancement may pose new safety risks. We study this problem by introducing MIR-SafetyBench, the first benchmark focused on multi-image reasoning safety, which consists of 2,676 instances across a taxonomy of 9 multi-image relations. Our extensive evaluations on 19 MLLMs reveal a troubling trend: models with more advanced multi-image reasoning can be more vulnerable on MIR-SafetyBench. Beyond attack success rates, we find that many responses labeled as safe are superficial, often driven by misunderstanding or evasive, non-committal replies. We further observe that unsafe generations exhibit lower attention entropy than safe ones on average. This internal signature suggests a possible risk that models may over-focus on task solving while neglecting safety constraints. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/thu-coai/MIR-SafetyBench.

papers.title: Analyzing the Noise Robustness of Deep Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Why are adversarial examples (slightly perturbed images) misclassified by deep neural networks, and how do the datapaths of adversarial and normal examples diverge and merge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a visual analysis tool, AEVis, which extracts and visualizes datapaths (critical neurons and connections) of adversarial and normal examples to explain the root cause of misclassifications.
papers.conclusion: AEVis effectively helps experts analyze the prediction process of adversarial examples and identify the root cause of misclassifications through multi-level datapath visualization and interaction.
papers.key_findings:
The datapaths of adversarial and normal examples diverge and merge at specific layers, revealing where and how the model's predictions change.
The root cause of misclassification can be traced to specific neurons or feature maps that fail to detect key features or are activated by adversarial noise.
A constrained datapath extraction method reduces randomness and better preserves diverging and merging patterns for comparison.
Multi-level visualization (network, layer, neuron) combined with contribution analysis enables systematic investigation of adversarial misclassifications.
Case studies on ResNet101 and a 6-layer CNN demonstrate the method's ability to identify failure modes such as missed object parts or spurious feature detection.
papers.limitation:
Time complexity of datapath extraction and contribution analysis (several minutes offline, ~5 seconds for contribution analysis).
Visual scalability for very deep CNNs (thousands of layers) and when comparing many datapaths.
Generalization to other DNN types (RNNs, AEs, DGMs) and data types (text, video) requires extension of datapath extraction and visualization methods.
future_direction: Develop targeted defense solutions based on discovered root causes of misclassification.
Enable online detection and monitoring of adversarial examples with streaming visualizations.
Generalize AEVis to analyze other types of DNNs (RNNs, autoencoders, generative models) and data types (text, video).
papers.abstract: Adversarial examples, generated by adding small but intentionally imperceptible perturbations to normal examples, can mislead deep neural networks (DNNs) to make incorrect predictions. Although much work has been done on both adversarial attack and defense, a fine-grained understanding of adversarial examples is still lacking. To address this issue, we present a visual analysis method to explain why adversarial examples are misclassified. The key is to compare and analyze the datapaths of both the adversarial and normal examples. A datapath is a group of critical neurons along with their connections. We formulate the datapath extraction as a subset selection problem and solve it by constructing and training a neural network. A multi-level visualization consisting of a network-level visualization of data flows, a layer-level visualization of feature maps, and a neuron-level visualization of learned features, has been designed to help investigate how datapaths of adversarial and normal examples diverge and merge in the prediction process. A quantitative evaluation and a case study were conducted to demonstrate the promise of our method to explain the misclassification of adversarial examples.

papers.title: Interpreting and Improving Adversarial Robustness of Deep Neural Networks With Neuron Sensitivity
papers.research_question: How does neuron sensitivity relate to adversarial robustness, and can stabilizing sensitive neurons improve model robustness against adversarial examples?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces neuron sensitivity as a measure for adversarial robustness and proposes the Sensitive Neuron Stabilizing (SNS) method to improve robustness by stabilizing the behaviors of sensitive neurons.
papers.conclusion: Neuron sensitivity is closely related to adversarial robustness, and stabilizing sensitive neurons can effectively improve model robustness against adversarial examples.
papers.key_findings:
Sensitive neurons (those with high behavior variation between benign and adversarial examples) make the most non-trivial contributions to model misclassification in adversarial settings.
State-of-the-art adversarial training methods improve model robustness by reducing neuron sensitivities.
Stabilizing sensitive neurons via the proposed SNS method effectively improves adversarial robustness across various datasets and attack methods.
There exists a trade-off between robustness and accuracy, and sensitive neurons are responsible for both clean accuracy and robustness.
Adversarial attacks exploit sensitive neurons differently at different layers, with bottom layers focusing on common low-level features and top layers on class-specific features.
papers.limitation:
Uses the same coefficient λ to combine sensitivities in different layers, which might not be optimal due to heterogeneous behaviors of different layers.
The layer selection method is a naive top-k procedure, which may not adapt well to various model architectures.
future_direction: Use adaptive coefficients that consider heterogeneous behaviors of different layers to make full use of each intermediate layer.
Develop a better layer selection strategy that adapts to various model architectures.
papers.abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are vulnerable to adversarial examples where inputs with imperceptible perturbations mislead DNNs to incorrect results. Despite the potential risk they bring, adversarial examples are also valuable for providing insights into the weakness and blind-spots of DNNs. Thus, the interpretability of a DNN in the adversarial setting aims to explain the rationale behind its decision-making process and makes deeper understanding which results in better practical applications. To address this issue, we try to explain adversarial robustness for deep models from a new perspective of neuron sensitivity which is measured by neuron behavior variation intensity against benign and adversarial examples. In this paper, we first draw the close connection between adversarial robustness and neuron sensitivities, as sensitive neurons make the most non-trivial contributions to model predictions in the adversarial setting. Based on that, we further propose to improve adversarial robustness by stabilizing the behaviors of sensitive neurons. Moreover, we demonstrate that state-of-the-art adversarial training methods improve model robustness by reducing neuron sensitivities, which in turn confirms the strong connections between adversarial robustness and neuron sensitivity. Extensive experiments on various datasets demonstrate that our algorithm effectively achieves excellent results. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to study adversarial robustness using neuron sensitivities.

papers.title: Feature-Guided SAE Steering for Refusal-Rate Control using Contrasting Prompts
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used with a systematic feature selection method to steer large language models for improved safety (refusal rate) without sacrificing utility?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method using contrasting prompts and a composite scoring function to systematically select Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features for steering, achieving simultaneous safety and utility improvements on Llama-3 8B without model retraining.
papers.conclusion: Feature-guided SAE steering is a viable and efficient approach to improving LLM safety without sacrificing utility, providing a foundation for mechanistically-informed safety alignment.
papers.key_findings:
A composite scoring method using contrasting prompts can identify SAE features causally related to refusal behavior.
Steering the top-ranked feature (Feature 35831) improved safety performance by 18.9% and utility by 11.1%, overcoming the traditional safety-utility tradeoff.
The method provides a computationally efficient alternative to traditional safety alignment methods like RLHF and Constitutional AI, which require extensive retraining.
papers.limitation:
The evaluation is restricted to Llama-3 8B and Layer 25, limiting understanding of scaling behaviors across architectures and transformer depths.
Reliance on automatic judges (GPT-4o for AirBench, GPT-4 for AlpacaEval 2.0) introduces potential limitations despite demonstrated correlation with human preferences.
The absence of direct comparisons with alternative steering methods limits the ability to establish relative effectiveness claims.
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) deployment requires guiding the LLM to recognize and not answer unsafe prompts while complying with safe prompts. Previous methods for achieving this require adjusting model weights along with other expensive procedures. While recent advances in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have enabled interpretable feature extraction from LLMs, existing approaches lack systematic feature selection methods and principled evaluation of safety-utility tradeoffs. We explored using different steering features and steering strengths using Sparse Auto Encoders (SAEs) to provide a solution. Using an accurate and innovative contrasting prompt method with the AI-Generated Prompts Dataset from teknium/OpenHermes-2p5-Mistral-7B and Air Bench eu-dataset to efficiently choose the best features in the model to steer, we tested this method on Llama-3 8B. We conclude that using this method, our approach achieves an 18.9% improvement in safety performance while simultaneously increasing utility by 11.1%, demonstrating that targeted SAE steering can overcome traditional safety-utility tradeoffs when optimal features are identified through principled selection methods.

papers.title: The Rogue Scalpel: Activation Steering Compromises LLM Safety
papers.research_question: Does activation steering, a technique for precise and interpretable model control, compromise LLM safety by systematically breaking alignment safeguards?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering, a technique promoted for precise and interpretable model control, systematically breaks LLM alignment safeguards, enabling harmful compliance even with random or semantically benign steering vectors.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering poses systematic safety risks by breaking alignment safeguards, even with benign vectors, challenging the paradigm of safety through interpretability. Mitigation strategies and further research into the underlying mechanisms are needed.
papers.key_findings:
Steering in a random direction can increase the probability of harmful compliance from 0% to 1–13% across different model families.
Steering with benign SAE features demonstrates comparable or greater harmful potential, increasing compliance by 1–4% over random steering.
Steering is most effective when applied to the model's middle or early layers, indicating safety mechanisms are most vulnerable in intermediate processing stages.
Most SAE features exhibit jailbreaking capabilities, but they show poor cross-prompt generalization, making systematic safety monitoring challenging.
Averaging just 20 random vectors that jailbreak a single prompt creates a universal attack vector that significantly boosts harmful compliance on unseen requests, requiring only black-box steering access.
future_direction: Investigate the mechanisms behind alignment failures by analyzing activation patterns or refusal circuits in the model’s latent space.
Develop mitigation strategies like adversarial training to counter steering perturbations.
papers.abstract: Activation steering is a promising technique for controlling LLM behavior by adding semantically meaningful vectors directly into a model's hidden states during inference. It is often framed as a precise, interpretable, and potentially safer alternative to fine-tuning. We demonstrate the opposite: steering systematically breaks model alignment safeguards, making it comply with harmful requests. Through extensive experiments on different model families, we show that even steering in a random direction can increase the probability of harmful compliance from 0% to 1-13%. Alarmingly, steering benign features from a sparse autoencoder (SAE), a common source of interpretable directions, demonstrates a comparable harmful potential. Finally, we show that combining 20 randomly sampled vectors that jailbreak a single prompt creates a universal attack, significantly increasing harmful compliance on unseen requests. These results challenge the paradigm of safety through interpretability, showing that precise control over model internals does not guarantee precise control over model behavior.

papers.title: No Two Devils Alike: Unveiling Distinct Mechanisms of Fine-tuning Attacks
papers.research_question: While different fine-tuning attacks can all significantly compromise safety, do their attack mechanisms exhibit strong similarities?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that two representative fine-tuning attacks (Explicit Harmful Attack and Identity-Shifting Attack) have distinct mechanisms for compromising an LLM's safety alignment, indicating the need for diverse defense strategies.
papers.conclusion: Different fine-tuning attacks exploit distinct mechanisms to compromise LLM safety, underscoring the need for varied and robust defense strategies.
papers.key_findings:
EHA aggressively disrupts the harmful instruction recognition stage by suppressing the transmission of harmful signals in upper layers, while ISA does not significantly impact this stage.
Both EHA and ISA disrupt the initial refusal tone generation, but EHA suppresses refusal tokens via MLPs in mid-layers, whereas ISA does not.
Both attacks impair the refusal response completion stage, with ISA having a greater impact, causing the model to persistently generate harmful content even with refusal prefixes.
Adding a safety-oriented system prompt only partially mitigates the impairment caused by the attacks.
The attacks cause representation shifts: EHA shifts representations more for harmful inputs, while ISA causes a shift orthogonal to the harmfulness direction.
papers.limitation:
The study only investigates two fine-tuning attacks (EHA and ISA), which do not encompass the full spectrum of possible attacks.
The analysis is conducted solely on Llama-2-7b-chat, limiting the generalizability of the findings to other models.
The investigation does not involve the mechanics of particular components (e.g., individual attention heads) due to scope constraints.
future_direction: Using trained probes at mid-layers to robustly detect harmful inputs without an external detector.
Developing more attack-resisting model manipulation methods for safeguarding, as current steering methods may be less effective on attacked models.
papers.abstract: The existing safety alignment of Large Language Models (LLMs) is found fragile and could be easily attacked through different strategies, such as through fine-tuning on a few harmful examples or manipulating the prefix of the generation results. However, the attack mechanisms of these strategies are still underexplored. In this paper, we ask the following question: \textit{while these approaches can all significantly compromise safety, do their attack mechanisms exhibit strong similarities?} To answer this question, we break down the safeguarding process of an LLM when encountered with harmful instructions into three stages: (1) recognizing harmful instructions, (2) generating an initial refusing tone, and (3) completing the refusal response. Accordingly, we investigate whether and how different attack strategies could influence each stage of this safeguarding process. We utilize techniques such as logit lens and activation patching to identify model components that drive specific behavior, and we apply cross-model probing to examine representation shifts after an attack. In particular, we analyze the two most representative types of attack approaches: Explicit Harmful Attack (EHA) and Identity-Shifting Attack (ISA). Surprisingly, we find that their attack mechanisms diverge dramatically. Unlike ISA, EHA tends to aggressively target the harmful recognition stage. While both EHA and ISA disrupt the latter two stages, the extent and mechanisms of their attacks differ significantly. Our findings underscore the importance of understanding LLMs' internal safeguarding process and suggest that diverse defense mechanisms are required to effectively cope with various types of attacks.

papers.title: LatentGuard: Controllable Latent Steering for Robust Refusal of Attacks and Reliable Response Generation
papers.research_question: How can we achieve robust safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) with fine-grained controllability and interpretability at the representation level?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces LATENTGUARD, a three-stage framework combining reasoning-enhanced fine-tuning with supervised latent space control via a structured VAE to achieve interpretable and precise safety steering in LLMs.
papers.conclusion: LATENTGUARD enables interpretable and controllable refusal in LLMs by integrating reasoning-aware fine-tuning with supervised latent space steering, achieving a favorable balance between safety enforcement and practical utility.
papers.key_findings:
LATENTGUARD significantly reduces unnecessary refusals on benign prompts (from 41% to 0%) while maintaining high refusal rates on adversarial prompts.
The method demonstrates strong performance against advanced attack strategies (Adaptive, PAP, DRA), improving refusal rates and safety scores.
Latent space intervention is most effective in middle-to-upper transformer layers (e.g., layers 13-17 for benign preservation, 15-23 for attack mitigation).
The framework generalizes across different model architectures, as validated on both Qwen3-8B and Mistral-7B.
Supervised latent disentanglement enables targeted manipulation of safety-related features (attack type, method, benign indicator) for controllable refusal behavior.
papers.limitation:
Depends on structured supervision signals (attack type, prompt category) from an auxiliary classifier; errors in this upstream model may propagate and degrade control reliability.
Focuses on MLP activations; extending to other components (e.g., attention) requires new supervision designs and may affect disentanglement.
Cross-architecture generalization of latent control remains open, especially for smaller or quantized models.
Real-time deployment demands efficient latent intervention and decoding strategies, which are deferred to future work.
future_direction: Scale the framework to larger models.
Extend it to unseen or evolving attack strategies.
Develop dynamic latent control schemes for real-time, context-sensitive safety interventions.
papers.abstract: Achieving robust safety alignment in large language models (LLMs) while preserving their utility remains a fundamental challenge. Existing approaches often struggle to balance comprehensive safety with fine-grained controllability at the representation level. We introduce LATENTGUARD, a novel three-stage framework that combines behavioral alignment with supervised latent space control for interpretable and precise safety steering. Our approach begins by fine-tuning an LLM on rationalized datasets containing both reasoning-enhanced refusal responses to adversarial prompts and reasoning-enhanced normal responses to benign queries, establishing robust behavioral priors across both safety-critical and utility-preserving scenarios. We then train a structured variational autoencoder (VAE) on intermediate MLP activations, supervised by multi-label annotations including attack types, attack methods, and benign indicators. This supervision enables the VAE to learn disentangled latent representations that capture distinct adversarial characteristics while maintaining semantic interpretability. Through targeted manipulation of learned latent dimensions, LATENTGUARD achieves selective refusal behavior, effectively blocking harmful requests while preserving helpfulness for legitimate use cases. Experiments on Qwen3-8B demonstrate significant improvements in both safety controllability and response interpretability without compromising utility. Cross-architecture validation on Mistral-7B confirms the generalizability of our latent steering approach, showing consistent effectiveness across different model families. Our results suggest that structured representation-level intervention offers a promising pathway toward building safer yet practical LLM systems.

papers.title: Probing the Robustness of Large Language Models Safety to Latent Perturbations
papers.research_question: What is the robustness of safety alignment in large language models to latent perturbations, and can minor shifts in internal representations trigger unsafe responses?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a fundamental lack of local robustness in the latent representations of safety-aligned LLMs, introduces a probing method and attack (ASA) to exploit this, and proposes a defense (LAPT) that improves robustness without harming general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Current safety alignment methods lack local robustness in the internal representational space, and robust AI safety requires fortifying internal representations rather than just modifying input-output behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Minor perturbations to hidden activations can successfully jailbreak safety-aligned LLMs, revealing shallow alignment.
The Activation Steering Attack (ASA) is an effective, lightweight jailbreak method that generalizes across models.
A gradient-based variant (ASAgrad) is even more effective by using harmful suffixes as targets.
Vulnerabilities are concentrated in specific 'fragile layers' within models.
Layer-wise Adversarial Patch Training (LAPT) can enhance alignment robustness against such latent attacks while preserving general task performance.
papers.abstract: Safety alignment is a key requirement for building reliable Artificial General Intelligence. Despite significant advances in safety alignment, we observe that minor latent shifts can still trigger unsafe responses in aligned models. We argue that this stems from the shallow nature of existing alignment methods, which focus on surface-level refusal behaviors without sufficiently altering internal representations. Consequently, small shifts in hidden activations can re-trigger harmful behaviors embedded in the latent space. To explore the robustness of safety alignment to latent perturbations, we introduce a probing method that measures the Negative Log-Likelihood of the original response generated by the model. This probe quantifies local sensitivity in the latent space, serving as a diagnostic tool for identifying vulnerable directions. Based on this signal, we construct effective jailbreak trajectories, giving rise to the Activation Steering Attack (ASA). More importantly, these insights offer a principled foundation for improving alignment robustness. To this end, we introduce Layer-wise Adversarial Patch Training~(LAPT), a fine-tuning strategy that inject controlled perturbations into hidden representations during training. Experimental results highlight that LAPT strengthen alignment robustness without compromising general capabilities. Our findings reveal fundamental flaws in current alignment paradigms and call for representation-level training strategies that move beyond surface-level behavior supervision. Codes and results are available at https://github.com/Carol-gutianle/LatentSafety.

papers.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
papers.research_question: Do induction heads constitute the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Presents evidence that induction heads, a type of attention head circuit, are the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads likely explain a large fraction of in-context learning in transformers, with strong evidence in small models and correlational evidence in large models.
papers.key_findings:
